anchor.title: Aerial View of Levittown, Pennsylvania (c. 1959)
anchor.creator: Unknown
anchor.citation: Unknown photographer. "Aerial View of Levittown, Pennsylvania." c. 1959. Via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LevittownPA.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white aerial photograph of Levittown, Pennsylvania, around 1959, showing row upon row of nearly identical mass-produced suburban houses stretching to the horizon.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows Levittown, Pennsylvania, from the air around 1959, with rows of nearly identical houses spreading out as far as the eye can see. Developer William Levitt used assembly-line methods to build thousands of affordable homes very quickly, creating one of the first and most famous suburbs in the United States. Many of the families who moved in were returning World War II veterans who could buy a home thanks to the low-cost mortgages guaranteed by the G.I. Bill. The image captures one of the biggest changes in American life after the war: the movement of millions of families out of crowded cities and into planned suburbs. The sameness of the houses became both a symbol of affordable prosperity and, to some critics, a sign of growing conformity.

anchor.title: New Mother Views Infant in Nursery, Loretto Hospital, New Ulm, Minnesota (c. 1959)
anchor.creator: U.S. Federal Government (NARA, NAID 558170)
anchor.citation: U.S. Federal Government. "A New Mother Views Her Child in the Nursery of Loretto Hospital in New Ulm, Minnesota." c. 1959. National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 558170), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_NEW_MOTHER_VIEWS_HER_CHILD_IN_THE_NURSERY_OF_LORETTO_HOSPITAL_IN_NEW_ULM,_MINNESOTA._THERE_ARE_TWO_HOSPITALS_IN_THE..._-_NARA_-_558170.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a new mother gazing through a glass window at her newborn in the hospital nursery at Loretto Hospital in New Ulm, Minnesota, around 1959, with rows of infant bassinets behind the glass.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows a new mother looking through a window at her baby in a hospital nursery in New Ulm, Minnesota, around 1959. Behind the glass, rows of bassinets are filled with newborns, showing just how many babies were being born at the time. The image illustrates the baby boom — the huge jump in births between 1946 and 1964, when about 76 million babies were born in the United States. As returning veterans married and started families, this wave of children would soon crowd schools, create new markets for family products, and reshape American culture. The photograph turns a giant statistic into a single, human moment between a mother and her child.

anchor.title: San Bernardino Freeway (I-10) Construction, Kelleg Hill, California (1957)
anchor.creator: Federal Highway Administration / U.S. Department of Transportation
anchor.citation: Federal Highway Administration / U.S. Department of Transportation. "San Bernardino Freeway (I-10) Construction on Kelleg Hill, California." 1957. FHWA Interstate Photo Gallery, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CA_51_I10_FHWA_1957_1663.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white 1957 photograph of earth-moving equipment and a freshly graded roadbed on Kelleg Hill in California, showing a deep highway cut during construction of the San Bernardino Freeway (Interstate 10).
anchor.caption: This 1957 photograph shows machines building the San Bernardino Freeway (Interstate 10) by cutting a deep path through a hillside in California. It captures the huge physical work needed to build the new interstate highways. President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, which created the Interstate Highway System — about 41,000 miles of road and the largest public works project in American history at the time. These highways helped suburbs grow, made long-distance trucking and travel faster, and encouraged a car-centered way of life. The reshaped hillside in the image shows how building the interstates literally changed the American landscape.

anchor.title: Drive-In Restaurant (NARA-547855)
anchor.creator: Environmental Protection Agency / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. "Drive-In Restaurant." c. 1970–1975. National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 547855), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DRIVE-IN_RESTAURANT_-_NARA_-_547855.jpg.
anchor.alt: Color photograph of a drive-in restaurant with cars lined up at carhop service stations beside a brightly lit roadside sign, illustrating America's car-centered fast-food culture.
anchor.caption: This color photograph shows a drive-in restaurant where cars are lined up so that customers can be served food without leaving their vehicles, next to a bright roadside sign. It illustrates the car-centered fast-food culture that took off in America starting in the 1950s. As more Americans owned cars and lived in the suburbs, businesses built drive-ins, diners, and fast-food stands designed for people on the go. The bright sign is meant to grab the attention of drivers passing by. The image shows how deeply the automobile shaped everyday American life — even changing how and where people ate.

anchor.title: Family Watching Television in Their Home (c. 1958)
anchor.creator: Evert F. Baumgardner / National Archives and Records Administration
anchor.citation: Baumgardner, Evert F. "Family Watching Television in Their Home." c. 1958. National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Family_watching_television_1958.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph by Evert F. Baumgardner of an American family — adults and children — gathered attentively around a television set in their living room, around 1958.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows an American family — parents and children — gathered around a television set in their living room around 1958. By the late 1950s, the TV had become the center of the home, with families watching programs together in the evenings. Television ownership jumped from about 9 percent of homes in 1950 to nearly 90 percent by 1960. This meant millions of families received the same news, entertainment, and advertising at the same time. The image shows how television reshaped family life and became the most powerful mass medium in America, giving advertisers and politicians a direct path into people's living rooms.

anchor.title: Elvis Presley Sworn into the U.S. Army, Fort Chaffee, Arkansas (March 25, 1958)
anchor.creator: Associated Press / Standard-Sentinel
anchor.citation: Associated Press. "Elvis Presley Sworn into the U.S. Army at Fort Chaffee, Arkansas." 25 Mar. 1958. Standard-Sentinel, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Elvis_sworn_into_army_1958.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white newspaper photograph of Elvis Presley and a roomful of young men raising their right hands to take the oath of induction into the United States Army at Fort Chaffee, Arkansas, on March 25, 1958.
anchor.caption: This newspaper photograph shows Elvis Presley raising his right hand alongside other young men as they are sworn into the United States Army at Fort Chaffee, Arkansas, on March 25, 1958. By 1958, Elvis had already become hugely famous for helping create rock 'n' roll by blending rhythm and blues with country music. His Army induction was front-page news across the country because he was the central figure of 1950s youth culture. The image captures the moment when the 'king of rock 'n' roll' joined the military, where he served from 1958 to 1960. It shows the meeting of rebellious youth culture and traditional duty.

anchor.title: President John F. Kennedy, White House Color Portrait (c. 1961–1963)
anchor.creator: Cecil Stoughton / White House / Executive Office of the President
anchor.citation: Stoughton, Cecil. "President John F. Kennedy, White House Color Portrait." c. 1961–1963. Executive Office of the President / White House, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:John_F._Kennedy,_White_House_color_photo_portrait.jpg.
anchor.alt: Color official White House portrait photograph of President John F. Kennedy, taken in the Oval Office by White House photographer Cecil Stoughton between 1961 and 1963.
anchor.caption: This official color portrait shows President John F. Kennedy in the Oval Office, taken by White House photographer Cecil Stoughton between 1961 and 1963. Kennedy became president in January 1961, and his 'New Frontier' program promised to fight poverty, address racial inequality, and win the Space Race. He was the youngest elected president and the first Catholic to hold the office, and his confident, telegenic style made him very effective in the new age of television. An official portrait like this was meant to make the president look both strong and inspiring. The image stands for the New Frontier era and connects to the documents in this unit on the Peace Corps, education, the Moon goal, and civil rights.
